G.Best Practices
1.Functional Family Therapy: The family therapy offered to these families will be a
modified versionof Functional Family Therapy, a best practice model.We've been trained inthis
model and find it very helpful for families asit generates hope and allows the family to look at the
problem behaviors from a different perspective.This change in perspective is crucial in that it
creates more flexibility in responding to the behaviors that typically caused relational and legal
problems.
Barton, Alexander, Waldron, Turner&Warburton(1985) ina study involving children
and adolescents at risk for foster care placement, FFTshowed a significant decrease in
rates of out-of-home placements, and a decrease in the number of contacts per case.
Gordon, Arbuthnot, Gustafson&Mc Green(1988) studied delinquents with multiple
offenses who were at riskforout-of-home placements.Theyfound that clients receiving
FFT had alower rateof recidivism and committed fewer offenses at a two year follow
up.Additionally those receiving FFT services had lower recidivism rates as adults.
Klein, Alexander, and Parsons(1977)demonstrated that siblings in families that received
FFT had a lower rate of court referrals than other treatments.
2.Mentoring: Mentoring hasbeen shown to be an effective intervention with juveniles.
This has also been our experience with transitioning youth.
}Child Trends (2002), a national research center, showed the following outcomes from
mentoring:
Positive academic outcomes, including better school attendance, increased chances
of enrolling in higher education, and more positive attitudes toward school.
Prevention of youth risk behaviors, including lower rates of substance use and
abuse, and delinquent acts.
Enhanced social and emotional development, including positive attitudes about the
future and the elderly, anincrease in helping behaviors, andbetter trust of and
communication with parents.
National Mentoring Center demonstrated thatyouth participating in mentoring programs
are:
27% less likely to start drinking
46%less likely tobecome involved with drugs
52% less likely to skip a day of school

64%develop more favorable attitudes toward school
56% report improved peer relationships

3.In-Home Services: There is a correlation between how often and where services are
offered with treatment outcomes.Offering services in the home greatly increases a positive
outcome.
·Brooks etal(2000)showed that increased rates ofin-home contact produced greaterage-
appropriate expectations, better family communication, n creased attention to the child's
needs, improved marital relationships, and an improvement in the child’'s willingness to
accept discipline.

Attachment 2: Brief History of Organization
Historyof Organization
Youth Alternatives is a department of the City of Cheyenne and is a government agency.The
program was established in1971 to provide services to youth placed on probation in the City of
Cheyenne. The program received national recognition as an exemplary Model Cities Project.
Congressman Teno Roncalio spoke about the program before Congress in1974 and in 1975 the
program was selected to appear in a book of exemplary projects.
In1977, the program received a letter of commendation from President Jimmy Carter and the George
Washington Honor Medalfrom the Freedom Foundation in Philadelphia. In1980, the distinguished
Jefferson Award, from the Jefferson Foundations was awarded to the program.
In1990, the program was recognized for outstanding volunteer achievement by President George
Bush and was designated as the 247h Point of Light and in 1991 the program received a medal
commemorating this honor at a ceremony in Florida.
Todate, our services have grown to include: family counseling, court services, pre-court diversion,
probation, juvenile alcohol&drug intervention program, electronic monitoring, work alternatives
program, group services, school services, family crisis intervention, community challenge course,
and Special Friends-our mentoring program.
Youth Alternatives provides the City of Cheyenne with a coordinated response to the needs of
troubled youth in the community.The program utilizes the community as a tool to modify the
inappropriate behavior of troubled youth.The program is designed to intervene in the lives of young
people at an impressionable state in their growth and curtail their continuance orentrance intothe
juvenile justice system.The program attempts toassist troubled youth to see themselves asbetter
people and the world as less hostile by providing preventative, supportive, and rehab il it at ive
services.

II.PROGRAM SUMMARY
In 2009, Laramie County had 122placements with an average of 86.25youth in placement,
which was the highest in the state. The average length of a placement was 307.12 days.Laramie
County has the most placement days (29,987) of any county in the state.Thirty five youth (28.69%)
returned to a residential facility, resulting in a second placement.
A great deal of time and resources arefocused on getting a child into anout-of-home placement,
but little on geting him out.This unbalanced approach significantly negates the initial time and
financial investment because noone helps thechild and family applyin their home what was learned
in the placement. We know times of transition are points of high stress, requiring extra support and
thoughtful interventions.Project H.O.M.E.willaddress this significant lapse in thejuvenile system,
increasing the success of integrating children back into their homes, schools and community.This
project will also reduce the number of youth returning to a second out-of-home placement by
providing theneeded support for the youth, family, and community.
Because of the need to reduce placements, the Department of Family Services came to Youth
Alternatives three years ago and asked if we would apply for funding to begina transition program.
Theinitial funding was for a half-time family therapist through a Family Preservation Grant and a
youth mentor througha Diversion Grant.Afterthe second year, thefunding forthe half-time family
therapist was reduced.Because we felt so strongly about the program, we continued to subsidize the
therapist to continue to work with the transitional families. We can no longer do that.We are thus
applying for funding for the half-time family counselor, and some mileage support.We curently
receive funding from another grant for the Youth Mentor.
It is thus our plan tomeet the goals ofthe Time-Limited Family Reunification Services
through Project H.O.M.E.
PROJECTH.O.M.E.
For the past three years Youth Alternatives has assisted youth to successfully return to their
home, school, and community.Because of our work with the returning youth and their families, we
believe we can r ovid e the needed energy, experience and expertise to reunify the child safely wit in
the stated timeframe, andreduce the number of second placements.
The acronym H.O.M.E.covers many of the program components:
H: Home - everyone in the home is eligible to receive supportive services. Support and
accountability for all family members increases the likelihood ofa successful reunification.
Additionally, the services will primarily be provided in thefamily's home.This increases
family participation, and improves the match between the need and the service provided.
Q: Others -Developing a supportive Core Team for the family who supports the reunification
home is critical to the family's success.Collaboration with others (family relatives, coach,
pastor, neighbor, scoutleader, D.F.S., District Attorney's Office, school ersonnel, andothr
community agencies)will be extremely helpful in providing wrap around services for the
family.This Core Team would be there for the family and provide meaningful support.

of the youth.Most returning youth don't have a positive peer group available, so they

placement.The mentor will bridge this social gap. Additionally, he mentor-youth

the student, keeping others aware of circumstances and progress, checking credit concerns,
and scheduling school visits.Keeping the youth in school is crucial to his/her long term

return to his/her home school are low.

B.Intent of the Program
The intent ofthe Project H.O.M.E.is to provide the needed services to successfully transition
the youth intohis home, school and community.Once the youth is home, the intent is to keep him
there.Thisis made somewhat more difficult due to the initial placement.Once that first placement
has been made, placement now becomes an option in the choices the parents and community
consider.Successful reintegration into the community negates the need for another placement.Our
staff would work diligently to help the youth return and find a place where he could be successful.
C.Geographic Area to BeCovered
Laramie County is the area of focus. As was noted earlier, much could be done to reduce
many of the statistics associated with placements.Impacting Laramie County would greatly reduce
the statebudget.
D. Lead Agency or Organization
Youth Alternatives is the lead agency.
E.Goals of the Program
As was stated earlier, the goal of Project H.O.M.E. is to provide Time-Limited Family
Reunification Services so the youth can be safely and successfully integrated back into his home,
school and community.
IHI.PROGRAM DESCRIPTION
A.GOALS/PURPOSES AND OUTCOMES
Project H.O.M.E.would provide the appropriate services needed to facilitate a positive and safe
reintegration of the youth intohis family.We have been very effective in helping youth get off
probation, obtain a job, be clean and sober, finish school or obtain a G.E.D., and move to a more
independent type of living arrangement like independent living, foster care or the Job Corps.
Over the past three years, we've come to more thoroughly understand the needs of those
involved in placement situations.
Youth Needs: Youth need more frequent(but usually briefer) contact in order tokeep
moving on their plan and to notrevert backto old behavior.This often means meeting them on their
turf, providing specific direction for specific situations and texting them and allowing them to text
the service provider. This approach has allowed a strong positive connection between the youth, the
mentor, and the family therapist.When this kind of connection is made, the probability of the youth
calling the mentor or the family therapist before making a poor decision is greatly increased.
Returning youth need significant support to make positive school choices.It has been
extremely difficult for themtore-connect with their home school.Their major way ofdealing with
this issue has been to avoid it when possible.We believe the reason for this struggle is the
disconnect between the youth and school people.Ways of keeping the home school involved
throughout the whole process needs additional work. It has been difficult to arrange school visits
concurrent with home visits.Funding and other issues interfere with adequate time for theyouth to
connect with the school when he/she is on a home visit.The youth and school personnel need to
have many contacts during the placement to increase the likelihood of a successful school

To solve the school problem, many youth have chosen to work on their G.E.D.instead of
going back to the public school. The Goal Program offered through our office and L.C.C.C.has

Kids need social connections.Upon their return, we've seenkids struggle with developing
new positive habits and social activities.The strong mentor relationship has allowed the youth to
avoid the social isolation while attempting to associate with a different peer group.Going to the
YMCA, getting assistance in finding ajob, and learning new social skills have been the focus of
many of the supportive activities.
Parental and Familial Needs: Parents need to be listened to and provided services that meet
their perceived needs. Many parents at this point are very tired and are looking for support and
direction relative to their specific needs.Parents have not wanted yet another round of regular
services, tying up several of their evenings. But they do want support. We've found that providing
customized services has suited many parents very well.This means in-home services are more
important than in-office meetings, and availability in the evenings or weekends when problems arise
are perceived as being significantly more helpful.Knowing the family therapist is available to
answer questions and mcet when needed has been appreciated by the parents.The family therapist
will have the flexibility to respond to the families relative to their needs.At one point, twoparent
group meetings were conducted to assist with specific transitional concerns. Once those issues were
addressed, the parents weren't interested in continuing with an ongoing group.
Community Support People Needs: Once a youth is placed outside of his home, many
people involved with him quickly become focused on the needs of other youth who are still in the
school or community.The community support people need brief concise updated information about
the placed student that provides direction and gives them a specific role or task to complete.Without
periodic updates on how the student is progressing, the school personnel don't have the opportunity
to shift their perceptions and personal feelings concerning the student, and then have an
understandably difficult time matching up with the student's progress when he returns.
School personnel, probation officers and other professional people need to be persistently
contacted with clear requests of how they might participate in the youth's reintegration home.

B. Key Components of Project H.O.M.E.
As stated earlier, the needs assessment data indicates that Laramie County places many youth,
for long periods of time, and often has to place them for a second time. The cost -emotionally,
financially, academically, and socially-is quite significant.Project H.O.M.E.has the following
key components:
>Proven Experience: We have been working with youth and their families on this
particular issue for the past three years.We also focus on families and family issues.We
use Functional Family Therapy (FFT) (best practice model) to understand and assist
familiesto understand and solve their problems.
>Family Expertise: Youth Alternatives has two clinical Members of the American
Association For Marriage and Family Therapists who hold Marriage and Family Therapy
Licenses through the state.Additionally one is also a certified Supervisor of Marriage
and Family Therapy. Youth Alternatives is a recognized training site for Marriage and
Family Internships through Colorado State University.Both licensed therapists have
written books on Family Therapy.
Family Systems Approach: Family tension, safety, resolving conflict, growing through
developmental stages, and transitioning in and out of the home are all family system
issues.All of the staff involved are family focused systems oriented individuals. We
understand families and can provide strength-based family assessments.
Strength Based Approach: Engaging struggling families canbe difficult.Approaching
from a strength basis is a best practice approach.This is not a new concept for us, but
a practiced skill of many years.
Community Involvement: It is crucialto develop a Core Team around these youth and
families.Typically there are many people who would bequite willingtobe involved, but
they need some structure and direction as to the role they could play.Coordinating the
community players would make all of the services much more productive.Because
Youth Alternatives has been in Cheyenne since 1971, we are connected with all of the
major providers of youth services.
Services Provided to Achieve Outcome
Forreferred families, the following services will be available:
1. Case Management: The family therapist and youth mentor will be the organizational hub
for the family, the services and the Core Team of individuals who are involved with the family.This
service will ensure that important dates and services are tracked and monitored. Progress will be
monitored and significant information will be regularly conveyed to D.F.S.personnel. The family
therapist will supervise the case manager and mentor.
